toc.title: Original mixed states and new ones
We're always in a mixed state
Fawn and appeasement as adaptations to shutdown and freeze
How I'd work with it in therapy

blocks.p: Fawn and appeasement are two of the three new mixed states added to the Polyvagal Theory. Intimacy is the third. In all honesty, I've struggled with conceptualizing fawn and appeasement in particular, and I want to share my thoughts with you, to get you thinking along with me.
My main question is: what is the best conceptualization for fawn and appeasement?
There are no test tubes here. There are no machines identifying what's happening underneath someone's behaviors. We are inferring, speculating on some level, and I think that's okay.

But when it comes down to it, no one is measuring someone's heart rate variability, or their baseline respiratory sinus arrhythmia, and then checking it again when they're under duress. If that is happening, it's in a lab, not day to day. I don't know of an objective way the polyvagal researchers have come up with to say, "When someone shows this type of behavior, these are the states going on, here are the specific measurements, here is the quantity of safety activation, here's the quantity of shutdown, and here's flight and fight."

So there's a lot of inference here. I think it's okay to discuss these things, and I want to add my own conceptualization. I'm wondering whether looking at fawn and appeasement as mixed states is the best way to look at them.

blocks.h: Original mixed states and new ones

blocks.p: Originally, we had the three primary states: safety, flight and fight, and shutdown. And we had three mixed states. I'm going to call those the original mixed states, to differentiate them from the three new ones.

When you combine the three primary states, you get the three original mixed states. But now we're looking at phenomena like fawning and appeasing and applying the polyvagal lens to them. It's not like someone was in a lab and found, "When we mix this with that, voilà, we get appeasement." It's more: here's a thing, and now we're inferring what's happening underneath what we see.
I do think the Polyvagal Theory has a lot to bring to the table here. I just don't know if looking at them as mixed states is the best way.

Fawn and appeasement have a lot of overlap. Both involve being in extreme danger, and I would say life threat scenarios, where there is a captor or an abuser and flight or fight is not an option. Both involve significant shutdown activation, including dissociation, and disconnection from one's values and from the empowerment of the self. Sacrificing everything, I would imagine, all of oneself, in order to survive a situation.
So would these be better framed as behavioral adaptations, rather than mixed states?

Just as a recap: a behavioral adaptation is a behavior someone does in order to reduce the experience or the intensity of their defensive activation. Typically it's in response to a stuck defensive state. Examples include self-harm, hair pulling, substance and alcohol use, cutting class, overworking: all kinds of things we do to relieve whatever we're going through.

If fawn and appeasement are behavioral adaptations, they'd be adaptations primarily to shutdown or freeze. We could look at them as behaviors, or behavioral groupings, in response to a predominant state: shutdown as a primary state, or freeze as a mixed state. I would speculate there's more of a flavor of shutdown.

blocks.h: We're always in a mixed state

blocks.p: Of course, there's always a mixed state happening. Right now, you and I are in a mixed state. I don't think we're ever in just one state, and we're probably always in all three primary states on some level.

As I record this, I'm sitting, and I'm talking. I'm moving my hands a lot as I talk. I'm also thinking critically. So I'm in safety, I'm in mobility, and I'm also in immobility. But I wouldn't say I'm in a mixed state called podcast recording. We wouldn't create a new mixed state to identify where I'm at. We'd say I'm doing a behavior, podcast recording, and I have primary states, and maybe a mixed state, underlying what I'm doing.

I do have a dominant flavor to my system, and it's probably safety. You could say I'm primarily in the mixed state of stillness, because I'm immobile but safe, with some mobility in my system. You could also argue I'm in more of a play mixed state, because there's a playful, co-regulative quality to what I'm doing. Either way, safety is involved in both. But no matter what you call my state, what I'm doing is podcast recording. You wouldn't call podcast recording the mixed state.

We could look at the same behaviors, look at what's happening underneath, and come to different conclusions. I already illustrated that with podcast recording, which could come from play or from stillness.

Here's another example: cruel words. Maybe someone's making fun of somebody else, or you're yelling at your partner and say something you regret. Those same words could come from explosive rage, which would probably be the fight state. They could come from a bullying, rageful place, which might be the freeze mixed state with an underlying anger to it, or fight. Or we could say cruel things from a playful mixed state, like a comedian does. The same words can have different flavors, depending on the primary or original mixed state the person is acting from.

The primary states and the original mixed states are the foundation for the [SSIEC](piece:snb154-ssiec-state-sensation-impulse-emotion-cognition). That's something I created. It stands for state, sensations, impulses, emotions, and cognitions. The primary states and original mixed states flavor our experiences and lay the foundation for our sensations, impulses, emotions, and cognitions.

So maybe it's more useful to look at someone's behavior and infer the flavor of their system using the primary and original mixed states. All behaviors have an underlying mixed state, but we don't call the behaviors mixed states in and of themselves.

Bullying, for example, has observable behaviors. But we wouldn't say bullying is a mixed state. We'd say bullying has a dominant primary state, or a dominant original mixed state, driving the bullying behaviors, like frozen rage or a sympathetic fight state. My worry is that we're equating a behavior, or a grouping of behaviors, with a state or mixed state. I don't think they're the same.

blocks.h: Fawn and appeasement as adaptations to shutdown and freeze

blocks.p: So let's bring this to fawn and appeasement. I'm putting this to you, because I don't know the right answer, and it's where I've been stuck for quite a while. Is it more useful to conceptualize them as behavioral adaptations with an underlying primary state or original mixed state?
In my opinion, shutdown would be the underlying primary state, and freeze would be the underlying original mixed state.

I wouldn't call fawning and appeasing behaviors in and of themselves. They're more like behavioral groupings. There are a lot of things someone could do that we'd call fawning or appeasing. That general grouping of behaviors would be an adaptation to a dominant shutdown state or freeze mixed state.

Maybe this isn't that different from the current conceptualization of fawn and appeasement. But I think it's an important distinction: the behavior is different from the state that's underlying it and driving it.

blocks.h: How I'd work with it in therapy

blocks.p: When I work with somebody, I haven't spent time differentiating whether they're in a fawn state or an appeasement mixed state, and I don't think I would. Instead, I'd identify their primary defensive state, the one flavoring their decision making and their behavior.

For fawn and appeasement, that would be shutdown, because fawning and appeasing involve so much dissociation from the self and one's values, a lot of self-sacrifice, and disconnection from the present moment and from the self. The true self, if you want to call it that.

So we could identify that you, the general you, were probably in a dominant shutdown state. Then we could look at the behaviors that came from that shutdown state, like connecting with the captor and engaging with them and their goals. Those are more specific behaviors we'd call appeasing. And we could see that those behaviors probably came from shutdown. That's how I think in therapy: you adjusted your behavior based on the needs of the context, and more specifically, based on significant shutdown activation.

We could say you lied for the benefit of your abuser or your captor. But that lying helped you survive, and it probably came from shutdown, which got you to compromise your values. Maybe it even came from flight and anxiousness, and lying helped relieve the flight activation. We could say you prioritized the captor's needs in order to survive. We could say you agreed with the captor's lies, or their gaslighting. But these probably stemmed from a significant amount of shutdown.

So we can take all those behaviors as a grouping and call it appeasement. I think they'd fit into fawning on some level as well. The primary factor is probably shutdown or freeze. All these behaviors come from it, and then we group those behaviors into appeasement or fawning, which each have their own flavor.

To take this a step further: all three states are always active at the same time. They are right now for me. But that doesn't result in appeasement. There's something different about appeasement, where all three states are active but the result is something different.

So instead of saying all three are active and there you go, maybe we should look at it as shutdown being the most dominant. When someone is in that massive shutdown state, it provides a sort of new platform they build off of. It puts them on autopilot. They're not really an active driver of their body, their decision making, their self. They're watching their life on autopilot, as if it's a movie. That's a very common description from people in a severe shutdown, dissociative state.

But even on autopilot, they're still able to function daily. I'm not saying it's great functioning, but they can get their needs met because of the shutdown autopilot. And they might even be using the biological pathways of the other states on some level.

The kids I work with in schools who are in a significant dissociative shutdown state are mobile enough to get to school. They're mobile enough to smile their way through interactions they don't want to be part of, or can't be a genuine part of. That significant shutdown seems to put them on an autopilot where they can get through the day. I'm not saying it's a great quality of life, and I don't encourage you to strive for it. But it provides this new autopilot platform. That's the best word I have for it at this time.

I would not call autopilot a mixed state. To me, it's more of a function of being in significant shutdown. And if this conceptualization is helpful, I wonder how much it has to do with dissociative identity disorder. How many times can the mind go on autopilot, create a new platform, and then switch between them? I don't know. I'm purely speculating.

So could we look at fawning and appeasement as significant shutdown states that put somebody on this autopilot, one that really disconnects them from their values, from what they know is right or wrong, and from their inner power to act on that knowing and hold healthy boundaries?
This isn't an issue of blame. I think people do these things as a means of survival, and I don't blame them whatsoever. I don't think people are choosing to do this at all.

To get back to the point: I don't know if looking at fawning and appeasement as mixed states in and of themselves is the best way to look at them. Or we could look at them as mixed states with a more dominant flavor of a primary state or original mixed state, like shutdown or freeze.

If not, what does mixed state mean anymore? It seems to have lost its meaning. We're always in a mixed state. Any behavior, or grouping of behaviors, has an underlying mixed state. The person who's bullying, the person who's addicted to something: there's a mixed state going on. But we wouldn't call their state addiction. We wouldn't call their state bullying. There's a mixed state underlying it that's driving the addiction or the bullying.

It might be more useful to identify the predominant flavor of someone's system, and see the behaviors as coming from that predominant flavor, as a way to adapt to whatever they're going through. In my opinion, we don't need to keep adding mixed states to the Polyvagal Theory. This is not Dr. Porges's stance, or the stance he and his son take in Our Polyvagal World, and it's not the Polyvagal Institute's. This is just me speculating and wondering. Honestly, I think it's a more useful way of looking at things.

That said, I know other mammals have been shown to do appeasing behaviors. So maybe appeasement is more of a true mixed state, and not just a grouping of behaviors or a behavioral adaptation. Fawning seems distinct to me. It seems more like a behavioral adaptation to an ongoing stuck defensive state. Appeasement seems like it can be something immediate, but also a long-term adaptation.

Again, I don't know the correct answer. I wanted to give you a new wrinkle and a new way of framing this, and let you know where I'm coming from. I look forward to the day when our watches tell us our respiratory sinus arrhythmia and heart rate variability, and maybe even which state we're in. We're not quite there yet.
